images.title: Samaira and Kabir ask their friends
images.purpose: Put the reporters' question and five different answers in front of the student before any counting: the data are plain spoken answers, not yet a table.
images.composition: Samaira (microphone) and Kabir (notebook) at the left asking one question in a bubble across the top, and five friends in a row at the right, each with a speech bubble giving a different number of hours.
images.exact_structure: Plain white frame, 1456 by 816. Every person is a flat figure: a white round head (radius 40, thin dark #2B2B2B outline 3 px, two dot eyes, a small smile, a dark #2B2B2B hair cap on the top half), a rounded-rectangle body 80 px wide and 205 px high (y 385 to 590), two dark #2B2B2B legs (24 px wide, y 590 to 740) and two thin arms. Every head centre is at y 340 and every pair of feet stands on y 740. QUESTION BUBBLE: a white rounded rectangle (corner radius 28, dark outline 4 px) x 40 to 1130, y 30 to 130, with a small triangular tail (x 100 to 160 at its bottom edge) down to a tip at (130, 288) just above Samaira's head; inside it, centred at (585, 80), the question How many hours a day do you spend watching TV? in dark #1F2937 bold sans-serif (40 px). THE TWO REPORTERS at the left: (1) Samaira, head centre x 130, body filled reddish purple #CC79A7, holding a microphone in her right hand (the viewer's right): a dark #2B2B2B handle 14 by 60 px at x 188 to 202, y 440 to 500, with an amber #E69F00 round head (radius 18) at (195, 425). (2) Kabir, head centre x 330, body filled teal #0072B2, holding a notebook in his right hand (the viewer's right): an amber #E69F00 rectangle 70 by 90 px at x 385 to 455, y 450 to 540 with a white strip (50 by 14 px) across its front and a thin dark outline. THE FIVE FRIENDS stand in one row on the right with head centres at x 590, 765, 940, 1115 and 1290, bodies filled in this order amber #E69F00, green #009E73, grey #6B7280, reddish purple #CC79A7 and teal #0072B2, arms down. Above each friend's head sits one white speech bubble (rounded rectangle 160 by 90 px, corner radius 22, dark outline 3 px, y 170 to 260, centred on the friend, with a small tail down to y 290) holding that friend's answer in dark #1F2937 bold (34 px); from left to right the five answers are 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 2 hr and 2 1/2 hr. In all there are 7 people (2 reporters and 5 friends), 6 speech bubbles (1 question and 5 answers), 1 microphone and 1 notebook. No count, no table, no total and no written name anywhere. Nothing else in the frame.
labels: How many hours a day do you spend watching TV?
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
a count of the friends, a table, a total or any answer to a question written anywhere in the frame
five bubbles that do not read 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 2 hr and 2 1/2 hr from left to right, or a bubble with a repeated answer
a name tag or any name written on a person
images.takeaway: People give different answers to one question, and the reporters will have to collect the answers and record them.
images.description: Two reporters ask the question How many hours a day do you spend watching TV? and five friends answer 1/2 hr, 1 hr, 1 1/2 hr, 2 hr and 2 1/2 hr.
images.context: Concept image for the hook. It follows the idea of the notebook of answers in your maths book (children with a bubble saying how many hours they watch TV) and shows only five of the answers, with no count and no table.
images.teaching_notes: Let the student read the five answers aloud and say how the reporters could keep them all. Do not count, sort or total on this picture. The slip to watch: reading the bubbles as one answer instead of five different ones.

image_decisions.why: The hook shows a question and five different answers before any counting, so the student sees why the answers need to be collected and recorded.
